issues.subcategory: Contradictory description of response format (open-ended vs. forced-choice)
issues.description: The Procedure and Analysis sections directly contradict each other regarding the format of the individual memory test. The Procedure states the test 'will contain 20 open-ended questions,' and the Analysis plan opening states the study modifies the original procedure 'concerning applying open-ended questions in the individual memory test.' Yet later in the Analysis plan it states 'In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.' These are incompatible response formats, and the entire scoring scheme (correct/misinformation/other) depends on which is used. This is a fundamental, unresolved contradiction that prevents evaluation or replication.
issues.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie... In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent number of critical details/questions
issues.description: The number of critical details and corresponding questions is internally inconsistent. The movie is described as having 'eight critical details.' The collaborative recall test is said to include 'four of which refer to critical details, with the other eight being control questions' (12 total), and 'each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details.' The individual memory test contains '20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details... regardless of whether they were subsequently discussed.' If only four of eight critical details are discussed, then four are non-discussed; but the design also claims items are 'fully counterbalanced.' Fixing the same four discussed items for all pairs contradicts the counterbalancing claim. The numbers and design statements do not reconcile.
issues.quote: In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.

issues.subcategory: Counterbalancing claim contradicts fixed item assignment
issues.description: The Design section states 'discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced,' but the Procedure specifies a fixed set of four critical details discussed by all pairs ('all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo'). If the same items are always discussed and the same items always non-discussed, discussed/non-discussed status is fully confounded with item identity, defeating counterbalancing and confounding item difficulty with condition. This is a serious design flaw for a within-subjects manipulation.
issues.quote: In the study, the memory conformity effect will be measured in a within-subjects design and discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis for replication uses implausibly small required sample
issues.description: The power analysis for replicating the memory conformity effect reports a required N of only 18 for 90% power based on a pooled Hedges' g of 1.13 (Cohen f = 0.57) and an assumed repeated-measures correlation of 0.07. The two source studies had markedly different effect sizes (g = 1.92 vs. g = 0.38), and combining them under random effects to claim a very large pooled effect is questionable; the within-subjects correlation of r = 0.07 is also unusually low and drives down required N. Relying on a tiny estimated N derived from heterogeneous studies overstates power and is not transparent about the sensitivity of the estimate to these assumptions.
issues.quote: Under such conditions, the sample size required for 90% power was 18. As a much larger sample was assumed, it can be stated that the power to detect the memory conformity effect will be sufficient.

issues.subcategory: Implausibly low assumed repeated-measures correlation reused across analyses
issues.description: A correlation of r = 0.07 between repeated measures (discussed vs. non-discussed items) is assumed for both the replication power analysis and the interaction power analysis. A correlation this low between two memory accuracy measures from the same participants is implausible and conveniently inflates the power for within-subjects/interaction effects (lower correlation increases sensitivity for within-subjects contrasts in some parameterizations, or distorts it). The justification ('based on the research described above') does not explain how this value was derived, and using such an extreme value is an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom affecting the entire sample-size justification.
issues.quote: A correlation r = 0.07 between repeated measures was assumed based on the research described above (Ito et al., 2019; Kękuś et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: Study underpowered for its own stated expected effect
issues.description: The authors acknowledge the chosen sample (N=240) gives 'excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones' (small effect requires 664). Yet the interventions are novel, untested for two of three methods, and prior warning research produced inconsistent/null effects, and reinforced self-affirmation previously did NOT significantly reduce memory conformity. A small true effect is plausible, meaning the study is likely underpowered to detect the realistic effect size, risking inconclusive null results. The planned pairwise comparisons require even larger N (492 for small effects), exacerbating this.
issues.quote: Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

issues.subcategory: Confounded interventions varying on multiple dimensions
issues.description: The three interventions differ from one another and from control on multiple uncontrolled dimensions simultaneously (content, modality, active task engagement). For instance, the Demonstration and motivation condition includes an active DRM task with personalized feedback plus a motivational podcast, whereas Education about memory and Extended warning are passive ~7-minute podcasts, and control is an unrelated soft-skills podcast. Differences in active engagement, time-on-task, and arousal are confounded with the theoretical content, so any group differences cannot be attributed to the hypothesized mechanisms. The authors themselves note overlap among interventions but do not control these confounds.
issues.quote: Secondly, we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.subcategory: Control condition not matched on demonstration/engagement
issues.description: The control group listens to a passive podcast about soft skills, which does not match the experimental conditions on engagement, the act of completing a memory task (DRM), or receiving any memory-related framing. Without an active control matched on task structure and time-on-task, observed effects could be attributable to nonspecific factors (e.g., increased general alertness, demand characteristics) rather than the specific manipulations. This weakens causal inference about which mechanism produces any effect.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: DRM false recall does not validly demonstrate susceptibility to co-witness misinformation
issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation method uses DRM false recall to 'demonstrate the fallibility of memory,' assuming this generalizes to make participants resistant to co-witness misinformation. DRM false memory (internally generated semantic associates) and social/co-witness misinformation susceptibility are distinct phenomena with weak or no established correlation. Using DRM performance as both a demonstration of relevant vulnerability and (in exploratory analysis) a predictor of MORI conformity assumes a construct overlap that is not established, threatening the validity of the manipulation's intended mechanism.
issues.quote: Demonstrating the individual fallibility of memory should make the participants alert to the real possibility that their reports may be distorted as a result of a discussion with the partner.

issues.subcategory: Scripted DRM feedback presupposes specific lures were recalled
issues.description: The scripted DRM feedback names specific critical lures ('doctor, window, sweet, thief') and tells all participants 'If so, you were fooled.' But DRM false recall is probabilistic; some participants will not have recalled these lures, in which case the 'demonstration' of personal vulnerability fails for them, undermining the manipulation's core premise (breaking the illusion of invulnerability). The manuscript does not address how the manipulation works for participants who did not produce false memories, nor verify the demonstration's success per participant.
issues.quote: See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief. If so, you were fooled.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between stated four discussed lists and four named lure words
issues.description: The DRM procedure states 'Four lists will be chosen' and the feedback names four lure words (doctor, window, sweet, thief), but only one example list (associated with 'doctor') is provided. The materials for the other three lists, their lure strengths, and the basis for claiming they 'produce the strongest effect' in 'our previous research' are not reported, preventing replication and evaluation of whether the demonstration will reliably work.
issues.quote: Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect.

issues.subcategory: Non-independence of paired participants not addressed in analysis
issues.description: Participants are run and tested in pairs (dyads) who jointly discuss items, creating statistical non-independence (shared discussion content, mutual influence). The analysis plan treats participants as independent units in ANOVA without any mention of accounting for dyadic dependency (e.g., multilevel modeling or treating the dyad as the unit). Ignoring this clustering inflates Type I error and violates ANOVA independence assumptions. The sample size of '240 participants (120 pairs)' further conflates the effective N.
issues.quote: Thus, analyzing memory conformity is based on a within-subjects factor... The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels

issues.subcategory: Discussed items assumed to contain misinformation without verification
issues.description: The scoring assumes 'all discussed items as having contained misinformation' simply because the procedure is designed to expose differing versions. However, participants may not actually have provided/exchanged the differing detail during free discussion (e.g., one partner may not mention the detail, or may guess the other's version). Treating all discussed items as misinformation-exposed without coding the audio-recorded discussions for actual exposure introduces measurement error and may inflate apparent conformity. The audio is recorded but the plan does not commit to verifying actual misinformation delivery per item.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.subcategory: Multiple outcome indices and comparisons without correction or primary outcome designation
issues.description: The analysis plan specifies four indices (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total answers) plus accuracy on filler/non-discussed/discussed questions, plus confidence ratings, plus DRM as predictor, plus hypothesis-awareness analyses, and planned pairwise comparisons among four groups with directional tests. No primary outcome is designated and no correction for multiple comparisons is specified, creating substantial researcher degrees of freedom and inflated familywise Type I error. For a registered report, the lack of a clearly prioritized confirmatory test and correction strategy is a notable gap.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.subcategory: Directional (one-tailed) tests assumed despite stated risk of opposite effects
issues.description: The power analysis assumes 'directional significance tests,' i.e., one-tailed tests for the interaction and pairwise comparisons. Yet the authors repeatedly acknowledge that the interventions could plausibly increase memory conformity (e.g., decreased confidence raising suggestibility; demonstrating fallibility leading to reliance on others). Using one-tailed tests when effects in the opposite direction are theoretically plausible is inappropriate and inflates Type I error in the predicted direction while making opposite (potentially harmful) effects undetectable as significant.
issues.quote: Comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.subcategory: Mechanistic claims (informational influence) not directly measured
issues.description: The authors build hypotheses around informational influence and the IMP 'consistency assumption,' and claim normative influence is 'completely ruled out' because the test is individual. However, the design does not directly measure participants' memory states, source monitoring, or awareness of discrepancies (the moderating variable central to all hypotheses), so the proposed mechanism cannot be tested. Claiming normative impact is 'completely ruled out' overstates certainty—prior social influence can carry over and individuals may still answer to remain consistent with the partner's stated view. The mechanistic framing exceeds what the measures can support.
issues.quote: we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.subcategory: Key moderator (awareness of discrepancies) central to hypotheses but not operationalized
issues.description: The entire theoretical rationale predicts effects 'will be higher among people aware of discrepancies than among those unaware,' yet the Methods/Analysis provide no procedure to measure each participant's awareness of discrepancies between original and post-event information. Without operationalizing this moderator, the central prediction cannot be tested, and the interpretation of any null or positive result is undermined. This is a major reporting/design gap given the emphasis placed on the moderator.
issues.quote: we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on materials, counterbalancing, and randomization implementation
issues.description: Several elements needed for replication are missing: the specific content/scripts of the podcasts; how movie versions are assigned within pairs and counterbalanced across the eight critical details; the randomization method for assigning pairs to four groups; how 'other answers' will be coded reliably for open-ended responses (inter-rater reliability); and how disagreements during discussion ('both responses documented') are handled in scoring. These omissions prevent full evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups

issues.subcategory: Vague exclusion criteria and no missing-data plan
issues.description: The only stated exclusion is 'any technical problems during the experimental session,' which is undefined and grants discretion (researcher degree of freedom). There is no plan for handling participants who fail the MORI deception (e.g., notice they saw a different movie or 'peek'), guess the hypothesis (collected but only 'exploratory'), produce no DRM false memories, or have missing item responses. For a registered report, predefined handling of these contingencies and missing data is expected and absent.
issues.quote: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.subcategory: No manipulation check for MORI deception success
issues.description: The validity of the MORI paradigm depends on participants believing they watched the same movie (not noticing the dual projection). No manipulation check is described to verify that participants remained unaware of the deception, nor a rule for excluding pairs in which the illusion failed. Without this, contamination of the conformity measure by suspicious participants is unaddressed.
issues.quote: the participants sit beside each other, look at the same screen, and are not aware that the other person is watching a different version.

issues.subcategory: Restricted age range and self-selected sample limit generalizability
issues.description: The sample is restricted to ages 16–35, recruited via media/internet advertisements (self-selected), and drawn from a Polish population. Eyewitness conformity and the efficacy of debiasing interventions may differ for older adults, children, and other populations relevant to forensic practice. While the age restriction is justified to avoid age-pairing confounds, the manuscript frames implications broadly for 'justice systems' without acknowledging that findings may not generalize to the age groups and naturalistic conditions most relevant to real eyewitness cases.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.subcategory: Ordinal efficacy predictions weakly justified
issues.description: The authors predict a specific rank ordering of efficacy (Demonstration and motivation > Extended warning > Education about memory) based on tentative reasoning ('we tentatively assume') and the fact that warning produced inconsistent results elsewhere. Given that two of three methods are entirely novel with no prior data, and the overlap among interventions is acknowledged, the directional ordinal hypotheses are weakly grounded yet are paired with directional (one-tailed) testing, compounding the analytic-flexibility concern.
issues.quote: the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.subcategory: Confidence rating scale labeled as guessing baseline at 0% misrepresents two-choice format
issues.description: Participants rate certainty from 0% ('complete uncertainty, guessing') to 100%. If the test is two-alternative forced-choice (as stated elsewhere), the chance/guessing baseline is 50%, not 0%, so a 0–100% certainty scale anchored at 'guessing = 0%' mismatches the response format and may distort confidence measurement and confidence–accuracy calibration analyses. This compounds the unresolved open-ended vs. forced-choice contradiction.
issues.quote: the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).

issues.subcategory: Pre-registration/timeline and analysis decision rules incomplete
issues.description: As a Stage 1 registered report, the manuscript should fully specify decision rules linking outcomes to hypothesis corroboration, including how a 'significant main interaction' triggers which specific pairwise comparisons, the exact model specifications, handling of the four indices as separate vs. corrected tests, and criteria for declaring each method effective. The timeline statement is also internally odd (study and resubmission both 'no later than 2023'). These gaps reduce the constraining power of the registration.
issues.quote: If the Stage 1 review is accepted, the resubmission should be completed no later than in 2023.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent count of collaborative recall items vs. memory test critical items
issues.description: The collaborative recognition test has 12 questions (4 critical + 8 control), with five possible responses each, while the individual memory test has 20 questions (8 critical), and elsewhere the forced-choice format implies two alternatives. The shifting numbers of response options (five in collaborative recall, two-alternative in individual test) and item counts across phases are not reconciled, making the relationship between discussed details and tested details ambiguous and hindering replication.
issues.quote: Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer.
